newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Drnovsek appeals for Slovenia parliament support.
newsitem.headline: Drnovsek appeals for Slovenia parliament support.

text.p: Janez Drnovsek on Wednesday appealed to parliament to back him for a second term as Slovenia's prime minister after a defector from a rightwing party offered him a vital one-vote margin in parliament.
Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats won 25 seats of parliament's 90 seats in November's general election, which was Slovenia's second since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
During two months of negotiations, Drnovsek, who was president of Yugoslavia from 1989 to 1990, secured 20 votes from smaller parties, including the former communists.
But an absolute majority of 46 appeared to elude him until Ciril Pucko defected from the Christian Democrats on Wednesday.
"We have economic and social problems that have to be solved not today, but yesterday...That is why I decided I would vote for Drnovsek," Pucko said.
A parliamentary vote had been scheduled for Wednesday morning but was postponed after the defection. It was not immediately clear if voting would go ahead later in the day.

"I am here to ask you for your support in the election for leader of a new government," Drnovsek told parliament in a pre-vote address. "I am sure that you will decide according to your conscience and with your full responsibilities to Slovenia's citizens."

Defending his economic record during four years in power, Drnovsek said he would strive to secure economic growth of between four and five percent a year and cut inflation to at least four percent from the current rate of nine percent.

Pucko's defection was certain to infuriate an alliance of three rightwing parties that had been confident of preventing Drnovsek from returning to power and of shifting Slovenian politics firmly to the right.

The alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, had won 45 seats in the election, and also needed one extra vote for an absolute majority.

Drnovsek, a committed pro-European, had crowned his four years in power by signing an association agreement with the European Union and vowed to reform Slovenia's economy, hoping for membership in 2001.

Slovenia, which developed into a stable democracy while other former Yugoslav republics were at war, won private assurances from Western governments that it could be a candidate for membership of NATO in its first expansion eastwards with the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.

The so-called "Spring" alliance had been banking on People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik, 36, being called to form a government in what it believed was the likely outcome of Drnovsek losing the parliamentary vote.
